text.text: Debates about reform in sport and exercise psychology research largely center on the shortcomings of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST) and the binary conclusions it produces.
We argue that significance testing is not the main culprit.
NHST matches our theories, which typically use boxes and arrows to state that an effect exists and in which direction.

So changing the statistical tool we use does not change much of what we learn, because it does not alter the questions we pursue or the specificity of the predictions we make: the answers we seek and settle for remain yes or no.

The good news is that sport and exercise psychology is in a strong position to tackle more informative questions: We have established that many effects exist, collected a wealth of quantitatively rich data, and have sophisticated methods at hand.
What is missing is a place in our theories to put these numbers.

We outline three increasingly ambitious levers to transform this foundation into a more quantitative body of knowledge: (1) treating effect sizes and their precision as primary targets of study planning and inference, rather than as decorative statistics reported alongside the p-value; (2) synthesizing evidence cumulatively, so that established findings such as expected effect sizes constrain the next study; and (3) formulating theories themselves more quantitatively, for instance regarding the shape of a relationship or how quickly an effect unfolds, so that they make more precise predictions.
Doing so benefits scientists and practitioners alike.
Theories that make precise predictions can actually be wrong, which is what makes confirmations meaningful.

A focus on cumulative effect size estimation also means that every well-conducted study teaches us something irrespective of its p-value, including the questions practitioners care about most: how much an intervention is likely to help, for whom, and when.
Quantitative data, qualitative answers "[T]he so-called test of statistical significance does not in fact answer a quantitative, scientific question.
… [B]y using Fisherian methods some of the putatively quantitative sciences have slipped into asking qualitatively whether there exists an effect….
They have ceased asking the scientific question of 'How much is the effect?'"
-Ziliak & McCloskey, The Cult of Statistical Significance (2008 p. 4f) Sport and exercise psychology is predominantly a quantitative science.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr">-Ziliak & McCloskey, The Cult of Statistical Significance (2008 p. 4f)</ref> Sport and exercise psychology is predominantly a quantitative science.

text.text: Its research operationalizes psychological processes as measurable variables and collects rich numerical data through psychometric instruments (e.g., questionnaires, rating scales), behavioral and performance metrics (e.g., reaction time, accuracy), and physiological and neuronal recordings (e.g., heart rate, brain activity).
These data are then analyzed with sophisticated statistical models (Biddle et al., 2001; Myers et al., 2018).
text.formatted: These data are then analyzed with sophisticated statistical models <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Biddle et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Myers et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This profile matches the conventional definition of the quantitative paradigm, which focuses on methodological and analytical properties of research (Creswell & Creswell, 2023).
text.formatted: This profile matches the conventional definition of the quantitative paradigm, which focuses on methodological and analytical properties of research <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Creswell & Creswell, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As the opening quote highlights, using quantitative machinery does not by itself make science quantitative.
What matters is whether the questions we ask, and the answers we seek, are quantitative too.
In sport and exercise psychology, our research questions and the conclusions we draw from our data are often merely qualitative, however, revolving around whether an effect exists.
The result is a large body of yesor-no answers that do not yet reflect the quantitative nuance achievable by numerical measurement and analysis.
Establishing whether effects exist is an important first step, and one the field has taken successfully in many areas.

This puts us in an excellent position to take the next one: asking how large these effects are and how precisely we can estimate them, and feeding these estimates into theoretical foundations that match the quantitative nature of our methods.
To take this next step, we first need to understand where the gap between our quantitative methods and our qualitative conclusions comes from.
One important factor is the field's reliance on statistical significance as its primary tool for scientific inquiry.

Under the dominant framework of null hypothesis significance testing (NHST), numerical data are used to compute a p-value: the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
If this probability falls below a conventional threshold, the null hypothesis is rejected; if it does not, the null hypothesis is not rejected.
Criticism of this procedure as a "statistical ritual" is almost as old as the framework itself (for reviews, see Cohen, 1994; Gigerenzer et al., 1989).
text.formatted: Criticism of this procedure as a "statistical ritual" is almost as old as the framework itself (for reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Cohen, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Gigerenzer et al., 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Even the architects of the frameworks that were later conflated into NHST would likely have objected to its contemporary application, in particular the rigid adherence to conventional thresholds and the idea that a single procedure suits every inferential goal (Fisher, 1956; Pearson, 1962).
text.formatted: Even the architects of the frameworks that were later conflated into NHST would likely have objected to its contemporary application, in particular the rigid adherence to conventional thresholds and the idea that a single procedure suits every inferential goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Fisher, 1956;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Pearson, 1962)</ref>.

text.text: In the words of Fisher (1956, p. 42), the pioneer of statistical significance testing, "no scientific worker has a fixed level of significance at which from year to year, and in all circumstances, he rejects hypotheses; he rather gives his mind to each particular case in the light of his evidence and his ideas."

text.text: More recent work has broadened this critique by emphasizing that p-values offer limited information on their own (Cumming, 2014; Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016), are widely misunderstood even by researchers with extensive statistical training (Goodman, 2008; Greenland, 2017; McShane & Gal, 2016 , 2017), provide fertile ground for questionable research practices (Simmons et al., 2011), and vary so strongly across exact replications that a single p-value is a poor guide to what a repetition would yield (Halsey et al., 2015).

text.text: These criticisms have resonated within sport and exercise psychology for quite some time (e.g., Andersen et al., 2007; Bernards et al., 2017; Büsch & Strauß, 2016; Thomas et al., 1991), and several problems that may partly stem from an overreliance on NHST have been documented, including p-hacking (D. N. Borg et al., 2023), unrealistically high rates of hypothesis confirmation (Büttner et al., 2020; Twomey et al., 2021), and disappointingly low replication rates (Mesquida et al., 2022 (Mesquida et al., , 2023;; Murphy et al., 2025).

N. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Borg et al., 2023)</ref>, unrealistically high rates of hypothesis confirmation <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Büttner et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Twomey et al., 2021)</ref>, and disappointingly low replication rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Mesquida et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Mesquida et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Murphy et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As important and worth discussing as these concerns are, they tend to draw our attention away from a much more fundamental problem.
When computed and reported properly, p-values behave exactly as they were designed to (Greenland, 2019; Lakens, 2021).
text.formatted: When computed and reported properly, p-values behave exactly as they were designed to <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Greenland, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Lakens, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The problem lies instead in their ritualistic use, in particular the widespread tendency to dichotomize substantive conclusions based on statistical significance (Amrhein et al., 2017; Hoekstra et al., 2006; McShane & Gal, 2016).
text.formatted: The problem lies instead in their ritualistic use, in particular the widespread tendency to dichotomize substantive conclusions based on statistical significance <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Amrhein et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Hoekstra et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">McShane & Gal, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The distinction between p-values and their use matters because dichotomization would persist even if all the criticisms mentioned above were addressed.
Suppose every researcher understood p-values correctly, chose thresholds deliberately and in advance, and avoided questionable practices thanks to well-designed incentives.
The output of the NHST procedure would still be binary.
However extensive the dataset and however sophisticated the model, the analysis culminates in a decision about whether the result is statistically significant.
The information loss is considerable:
Whatever precision a study achieves, whether through hundreds, thousands, or millions of observations, its central conclusion reduces to a single bit of information.
To be clear, such a formal decision procedure serves a legitimate and important function, as it allows scientific claims to be scrutinized and adjudicated (Tunç et al., 2023).
text.formatted: To be clear, such a formal decision procedure serves a legitimate and important function, as it allows scientific claims to be scrutinized and adjudicated <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">(Tunç et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: But if a binary decision were all we took away from our data, the whole enterprise would be remarkably inefficient.

Recognizing this, statisticians (McShane et al., 2019) and researchers across applied disciplines (Amrhein et al., 2019) have called for statistical significance to be abandoned as the primary criterion for inference and for evidence to be interpreted on a continuum, by estimating effect sizes and their uncertainty.
text.formatted: Recognizing this, statisticians <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(McShane et al., 2019)</ref> and researchers across applied disciplines <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Amrhein et al., 2019)</ref> have called for statistical significance to be abandoned as the primary criterion for inference and for evidence to be interpreted on a continuum, by estimating effect sizes and their uncertainty.

text.text: The primary inferential goal then shifts from hypothesis testing to estimation, a shift that has gained traction across sport science (Abt et al., 2020; Elkins et al., 2022; Schinke et al., 2021; Winter et al., 2014) and is equally warranted in sport and exercise psychology.

text.text: Moving toward estimation is an important step.
On its own, however, it is unlikely to close the gap between our quantitative methods and our qualitative conclusions, for reasons we turn to next.
Consider a typical sport and exercise psychology study.
An investigator compares a motivational intervention with a control condition on a cycling time-to-exhaustion task.

An a priori power analysis indicates that a sample of 128 participants is required to achieve 80% power to detect a statistically significant difference in time to exhaustion between conditions in an independent-samples t-test, using the default medium effect size of d = 0.5 and the assumption of equal allocation of participants to the groups.

Despite the considerable effort of running that many cycling trials to exhaustion, the study is conducted as planned, and the data analysis yields a statistically significant result, t(126) = 3.03, p = 0.003, d = 0.54, 95% CI [0.18, 0.89].
The investigator reports this together with a graph showing the raw time-to-exhaustion values in both groups, the group means, and their confidence intervals.
The discussion concludes that the findings support the hypothesis and that the observed effect is of medium magnitude according to conventional benchmarks.
Does this sound familiar?
It certainly does to us, as several of our own papers follow this or a similar template (e.g., Bieleke & Wolff, 2017; Wolff et al., 2018).
text.formatted: It certainly does to us, as several of our own papers follow this or a similar template (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Bieleke & Wolff, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Wolff et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: And measured against current calls for estimation, such a study appears to heed them.
But does it really?

Already at the design stage of the study, however, templates like this focus on maximizing the probability of obtaining a statistically significant result rather than on obtaining a precise estimate of the effect, reflecting a preference for hypothesis testing over estimation.
In line with this, the central conclusion is qualitative and rests entirely on a binary decision based on significance, while the estimates are reported but contribute little to the inference.

The effect size is merely assigned to a conventional category, a classification that Cohen himself considered a last resort (Cohen, 1988) and that ignores the specific outcome and research design (A. Caldwell & Vigotsky, 2020).

Caldwell & Vigotsky, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond offering a familiar label, the effect size has no bearing on the conclusion: had it been 0.4 or 0.7 and statistically significant, the hypothesis would have been considered supported all the same.
Similarly, the confidence interval is reported and plotted but not interpreted.
Whether it excludes zero is already implied by the p-value, so just presenting it adds nothing to the inference that the significance test has not already supplied.
Its more informative property typically goes unmentioned (Fidler et al., 2004): the interval shows the range of effects compatible with the data, which here spans from small to large.
text.formatted: Its more informative property typically goes unmentioned <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Fidler et al., 2004)</ref>: the interval shows the range of effects compatible with the data, which here spans from small to large.

text.text: Put bluntly, most of the statistics we report are merely decorative.
They appear in the results but get lost on the way to the conclusions.
Now consider a follow-up study.
Typically, it tests the null hypothesis again, asking whether the effect differs from zero.
At best, the estimate from the first study informs the power analysis; it does not enter the inference itself.
Inference thus starts over with the same yes-or-no question rather than accumulating quantitative knowledge about the phenomenon.

The tendency to draw qualitative conclusions is closely tied to the use of statistical significance as a general-purpose instrument of inference, although it can extend to other inferential quantities as well (Muradchanian et al., 2024).

text.text: Remarkably, the reliance on statistical significance persists despite decades of attempts at statistical reform and forceful calls to abandon it as the primary criterion for evaluating evidence.

Explanations for the slow pace of reform point to inadequate statistical training (Greenland, 2017), publication incentives that reward significant results (A. R. Caldwell et al., 2020; Franco et al., 2014; Tiller & Ekkekakis, 2023), or simply the inertia of established practice (Gigerenzer, 2018).
text.formatted: Explanations for the slow pace of reform point to inadequate statistical training <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Greenland, 2017)</ref>, publication incentives that reward significant results <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(A. R. Caldwell et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Franco et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Tiller & Ekkekakis, 2023)</ref>, or simply the inertia of established practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Gigerenzer, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A binary decision rule may also be easier to apply than interpreting evidence on a continuum, and it offers an illusory sense of certainty (Gelman, 2016; Gigerenzer, 2004).
text.formatted: A binary decision rule may also be easier to apply than interpreting evidence on a continuum, and it offers an illusory sense of certainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Gelman, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Gigerenzer, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these likely contributes, but all of them locate the problem outside the science itself, in researchers' training, incentives, habits, or preferences.

We argue that another reason lies within it: we settle for simple yes-or-no conclusions because most of our theories make equally simple yes-or-no predictions about whether an effect exists, not how large it should be.
The second part of this paper develops that claim.
"All models are wrong but some are useful." -based on Box (1976) In sport and exercise psychology, we routinely ask whether an effect exists.
text.formatted: "All models are wrong but some are useful." -based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Box (1976)</ref> In sport and exercise psychology, we routinely ask whether an effect exists.

text.text: Does motivational self-talk improve endurance performance?
Does mental fatigue impair subsequent performance?
Are people who are bored by sports less physically active?
These questions all share an important feature: they ask whether one variable affects or is associated with another.
This can be an important starting point for any research area (Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019).
text.formatted: This can be an important starting point for any research area <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: But imagine we would be asking instead how large an effect is, how quickly it unfolds, under which conditions it occurs, and how consistently it appears.
This might seem a trivial shift at first sight, but it opens up a substantially richer scientific approach.
Once the accumulated evidence allows, the field could move beyond the "whether" to refine its theories and make more specific claims.
In many areas, we have reached that point.

In psychology, a lively debate about a "theory crisis" has drawn attention to how theories are formulated and tested (Borsboom et al., 2021; Eronen & Bringmann, 2021; Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019; van Dongen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In psychology, a lively debate about a "theory crisis" has drawn attention to how theories are formulated and tested <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Borsboom et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Eronen & Bringmann, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">van Dongen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This debate has yet to gain much traction in sport and exercise psychology, although our theories share many of the features under discussion.
Most of them are verbal, often depicted as boxand-arrow diagrams.
The boxes represent psychological constructs and the arrows represent the assumed relations between them, usually intended as causal effects (Rohrer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The boxes represent psychological constructs and the arrows represent the assumed relations between them, usually intended as causal effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Rohrer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such diagrams specify which constructs are related and in which direction, and these relations are typically tested with NHST.
The theories remain silent, however, about the functional form of those relations or their temporal dynamics.
Consequently, a theory's evidential standing often depends only on whether an estimated effect has the predicted sign and differs from zero, not on its magnitude.
Testing such theories yields limited insights because they count a broad range of possible outcomes, namely every effect size in the predicted direction, as supportive evidence.

Paradoxically, when a theory predicts only whether and in which direction an effect occurs, greater precision through larger samples can make it harder, rather than easier, to refute it (Meehl, 1967 (Meehl, , 1978)): with sufficient power, even trivially small effects can be detected as statistically significant while remaining within the theory's predicted outcome space.
text.formatted: Paradoxically, when a theory predicts only whether and in which direction an effect occurs, greater precision through larger samples can make it harder, rather than easier, to refute it <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Meehl, 1967</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Meehl, , 1978))</ref>: with sufficient power, even trivially small effects can be detected as statistically significant while remaining within the theory's predicted outcome space.

text.text: Precision pays off only when a theory specifies what to expect, an issue that becomes ever more pertinent in the era of big data (Lin et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Precision pays off only when a theory specifies what to expect, an issue that becomes ever more pertinent in the era of big data <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Lin et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Clearly, such theories provide limited practical guidance, too.

Practitioners need information about the expected magnitude, uncertainty, and time course of an effect to make informed cost-benefit decisions, not merely to know whether an intervention "works" in principle (Lininger & Riemann, 2016), a conclusion sometimes based on the statistical significance of trivially small effects.
text.formatted: Practitioners need information about the expected magnitude, uncertainty, and time course of an effect to make informed cost-benefit decisions, not merely to know whether an intervention "works" in principle <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Lininger & Riemann, 2016)</ref>, a conclusion sometimes based on the statistical significance of trivially small effects.

text.text: A similar logic applies to the relations a theory leaves out.
An absent path is itself a claim: that one construct does not influence another.
In a fully specified causal structure such claims are testable, because each omitted relation implies a conditional independence that data can violate (Pearl, 2009).
text.formatted: In a fully specified causal structure such claims are testable, because each omitted relation implies a conditional independence that data can violate <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Pearl, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: In practice, these implications are rarely examined.

Moreover, the structure tends to bend to the data: when a predicted relation fails to appear, or when fit indices suggest that an added path or moderator would improve fit, we extend the model rather than treat the result as evidence against the theory.
Neither the arrows a theory draws nor those it omits therefore carry much commitment, and its structure resists refutation even before the question of functional form arises.

One might argue that quantifying the functional form of relations in sport and exercise psychology is not necessary, desirable, or even feasible, pointing to the complexity of human behavior and the limited precision of psychological measurement (e.g., Sanbonmatsu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: One might argue that quantifying the functional form of relations in sport and exercise psychology is not necessary, desirable, or even feasible, pointing to the complexity of human behavior and the limited precision of psychological measurement (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Sanbonmatsu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although human behavior is undoubtedly complex (Balagué et al., 2020; Schüler et al., 2025), whether it is more complex than the systems studied in other quantitative sciences remains an open question, and one we do not pursue here.
text.formatted: Although human behavior is undoubtedly complex <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Balagué et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Schüler et al., 2025)</ref>, whether it is more complex than the systems studied in other quantitative sciences remains an open question, and one we do not pursue here.

text.text: Our concern is with what the objection presupposes, namely that functional form can be left unspecified in principle.

Once quantitative methods are used, it cannot: every fitted model commits to a functional form, and even if the theory does not make that commitment, the analytic choice of model does so nevertheless.
The choice is therefore not between specifying a functional form and leaving it open, but between specifying it deliberately and specifying it by default.
Consider the linear model, which underlies most of the statistical procedures commonly used in sport and exercise psychology (Lindeløv, 2019).
text.formatted: Consider the linear model, which underlies most of the statistical procedures commonly used in sport and exercise psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Lindeløv, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Its estimated coefficient is read as the effect of X on Y:
This specification defines, by default, several aspects theories commonly leave open.
Each of them represents an opportunity for learning and advancing the field: a point at which a theory could become more explicit, and against which the data we collect could then be evaluated.
The first concerns the shape of the dose-response relationship.

The model assumes that each unit increase in X is assumed to be associated with the same expected change in Y across the entire range of X. This rules out all kinds of nonlinear relations, such as higher-order relations, thresholds, diminishing returns, or saturation.
Constant increments are an unlikely default for the processes we study.

Affective responses to exercise, for instance, do not decline smoothly with intensity but shift markedly around physiological breakpoints, the ventilatory threshold and the respiratory compensation point (Ekkekakis, 2003).
text.formatted: Affective responses to exercise, for instance, do not decline smoothly with intensity but shift markedly around physiological breakpoints, the ventilatory threshold and the respiratory compensation point <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Ekkekakis, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: As another example, effort and performance can decouple (Wolff, Hack, et al., 2026), and increasing levels of effort produce a convex rather than linear increase in performance, with markedly larger increments at high than at low or moderate levels of effort (Rewitz et al., 2024; Weilharter et al., 2024).
text.formatted: As another example, effort and performance can decouple <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">(Wolff, Hack, et al., 2026)</ref>, and increasing levels of effort produce a convex rather than linear increase in performance, with markedly larger increments at high than at low or moderate levels of effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Rewitz et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Weilharter et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such examples illustrate how theories would benefit from being specific about the shape of the dose-response relations they propose.
The second concerns temporal dynamics.
The linear model carries no time index and therefore describes a state that does not evolve.

The estimated coefficient is assumed to hold regardless of when measurement occurs, and effects that emerge only after a delay, accumulate, decay, or depend on prior states are not represented (Ryo et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The estimated coefficient is assumed to hold regardless of when measurement occurs, and effects that emerge only after a delay, accumulate, decay, or depend on prior states are not represented <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Ryo et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Research on boredom provides an example for this.
Boredom arises from a misfit between task demands and an individual's abilities, preferences, and energy level (Wolff et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Boredom arises from a misfit between task demands and an individual's abilities, preferences, and energy level <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">(Wolff et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As task demands change over the course of a performance, the degree of misfit changes with them, producing boredom trajectories that rise and fall within a single task episode (Rewitz et al., 2026).
text.formatted: As task demands change over the course of a performance, the degree of misfit changes with them, producing boredom trajectories that rise and fall within a single task episode <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">(Rewitz et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Capturing these trajectories requires more than the two moments a typical pre-post design records.
Boredom is not unique in showing such dynamics; comparable within-person fluctuations have been documented for other subjective experiences as well (Pérez-Díaz et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Boredom is not unique in showing such dynamics; comparable within-person fluctuations have been documented for other subjective experiences as well <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Pérez-Díaz et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Theories that specify when and how quickly an effect unfolds would bring these dynamics into view and also tell us when and how often to measure or intervene.
The third concerns differences between persons.

The linear model estimates a single slope assumed to hold for everyone, which is at odds with evidence that causal effects in behavioral sciences are typically heterogeneous (Bolger et al., 2019; Bryan et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The linear model estimates a single slope assumed to hold for everyone, which is at odds with evidence that causal effects in behavioral sciences are typically heterogeneous <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bolger et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Bryan et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: An average slope may therefore describe no individual in the sample, so a coefficient that is informative about a population can be uninformative about the person a practitioner is working with.

Averaging can even distort the functional form itself, as when individual learning curves that follow exponential functions average into a power function that describes none of them (Heathcote et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Averaging can even distort the functional form itself, as when individual learning curves that follow exponential functions average into a power function that describes none of them <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Heathcote et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, the coefficient is estimated from variation between people but interpreted as the relation the theory posits within people.
This inference holds only if all individuals follow the same process and that process is stable over time, a challenging condition for psychological processes (Molenaar, 2004).
text.formatted: This inference holds only if all individuals follow the same process and that process is stable over time, a challenging condition for psychological processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Molenaar, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: A theory that specifies not only the expected effect but also how much it varies across persons and conditions would turn this heterogeneity from noise into information (Bolger et al., 2019; Bryan et al., 2021) and make its generalizability explicit and testable (Yarkoni, 2022).
text.formatted: A theory that specifies not only the expected effect but also how much it varies across persons and conditions would turn this heterogeneity from noise into information <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bolger et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Bryan et al., 2021)</ref> and make its generalizability explicit and testable <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">(Yarkoni, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The fourth concerns everything the model leaves out.

Any other influence on Y is assumed simply to add to the effect of X, not to strengthen or weaken it, and the spread of Y around the predicted values is assumed to be the same at all levels of X. Most importantly, the model assumes that nothing it leaves out affects both X and Y, a crucial assumption for causal inference (Rohrer, 2018; Ruissen, 2024).
text.formatted: Any other influence on Y is assumed simply to add to the effect of X, not to strengthen or weaken it, and the spread of Y around the predicted values is assumed to be the same at all levels of X. Most importantly, the model assumes that nothing it leaves out affects both X and Y, a crucial assumption for causal inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">(Rohrer, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Ruissen, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This is the same commitment that the absent arrows in a path diagram make.

Many of us are aware of this limitation and avoid causal language especially in correlational work, sometimes at a reviewer's request, yet we often still draw causal inferences implicitly (Grosz et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Many of us are aware of this limitation and avoid causal language especially in correlational work, sometimes at a reviewer's request, yet we often still draw causal inferences implicitly <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Grosz et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A theory that explicitly names the plausible common causes of X and Y would tell us which variables to measure or control, and when the estimated relation can be read as a causal effect.
The four commitments can be relaxed, for instance, by elaborating the model (e.g., random intercepts or slopes) or by adding variables (e.g., covariates or moderators).
Each such step, however, requires a decision that a theory could inform but currently rarely does.
Contemporary theories predict that Y increases with X and leave everything else open.
As a result, the specification is settled at the analysis stage, on technical rather than conceptual grounds, and the resulting empirical claim is more specific than anything the theory asserts.
Every analytic choice we already make is thus a claim that a theory could make deliberately, and then test empirically.
As with effect sizes, theories that make qualitative predictions are indifferent to whether these assumptions hold.
Whether they are met is treated as a technical issue internal to the analysis: a violation prompts a different model, not a revision of the theory.

Effect sizes and findings about functional form therefore rarely make their way back into the theory, because a theory whose predictions are restricted to qualitative yes-or-no answers has no parameter to revise and no place to record a magnitude, a shape, a rate, or a degree of variability.
Estimates accumulate across studies, and meta-analysis pools them (Hagger, 2022), yet they rarely accumulate into theory, because the pooled estimate has nothing in the theory to update.
text.formatted: Estimates accumulate across studies, and meta-analysis pools them <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Hagger, 2022</ref>), yet they rarely accumulate into theory, because the pooled estimate has nothing in the theory to update.

text.text: Encouragingly, this means that the field already generates much of the quantitative information that more specific theories would require.
What we need are robust ways of feeding this information back into theory, and theories that can put it to good use.
We turn to both in the next part.

Asking better questions to find more relevant answers "Far better an approximate answer to the right question, which is often vague, than an exact answer to the wrong question, which can always be made precise."

-John W. Tukey (1962, p. 13, emphasis in original) All of this raises the question of how sport and exercise psychology can make fuller use of its quantitative potential to address more interesting and relevant questions.

text.text: We believe the field is in an excellent position to do so, and we see three levers, in increasing order of ambition: making better use of what we already have, consolidating the existing evidence and feeding it back into theory development, and making our theories' predictions more specific.
Figure 1 illustrates these levers and where they lead: the more specific a theory becomes, the fewer outcomes it can get away with, and the more it delivers to scientists and practitioners alike.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> illustrates these levers and where they lead: the more specific a theory becomes, the fewer outcomes it can get away with, and the more it delivers to scientists and practitioners alike.

text.text: Each lever moves theories further along this continuum, as we discuss in the following sections.

As outlined above, leading statistical associations (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016) and researchers across disciplines (Amrhein et al., 2019) have long called for abandoning statistical significance as the dominant, and often sole, criterion for evaluating evidence.
text.formatted: As outlined above, leading statistical associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">(Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016)</ref> and researchers across disciplines <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Amrhein et al., 2019)</ref> have long called for abandoning statistical significance as the dominant, and often sole, criterion for evaluating evidence.

text.text: The aim is not to discard p-values or significance tests, but to stop reducing evidence to a binary decision by default.

What takes its place is an honest and comprehensive account of what the data show, to which p-values, effect sizes, confidence intervals, measures of variability, and the data themselves each contribute.

Read as a continuous measure of how compatible the data are with a statistical model, a p-value remains informative (Greenland, 2019), and so do effect sizes, their confidence intervals, measures of variability, and the data themselves.
text.formatted: Read as a continuous measure of how compatible the data are with a statistical model, a p-value remains informative <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Greenland, 2019)</ref>, and so do effect sizes, their confidence intervals, measures of variability, and the data themselves.

text.text: Effect sizes and their confidence intervals, in turn, become primary targets of inference, telling us how large an effect is and how precisely it has been estimated (Cumming, 2014).
text.formatted: Effect sizes and their confidence intervals, in turn, become primary targets of inference, telling us how large an effect is and how precisely it has been estimated <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Cumming, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Binary decisions keep their place where a decision must actually be made (Tunç et al., 2023), but they need not be the default endpoint of every analysis.
text.formatted: Binary decisions keep their place where a decision must actually be made <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">(Tunç et al., 2023</ref>), but they need not be the default endpoint of every analysis.

text.text: In this sense, the first lever requires no new data and no new methods, only fuller use of the statistics we already compute.
As theories become more specific, they prompt better questions, rule out more wrong answers, and yield more useful predictions.
This shifts the focus from piling up statistically significant results to building genuinely quantitative theories, an evolution that characterizes maturing scientific disciplines.
Effect sizes become most informative when they are interpreted in practical terms rather than sorted reflexively into conventional categories (Andersen et al., 2007; A. Caldwell & Vigotsky, 2020).
text.formatted: Effect sizes become most informative when they are interpreted in practical terms rather than sorted reflexively into conventional categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Andersen et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">A. Caldwell & Vigotsky, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Measures with a natural metric, such as minutes of activity or repetitions completed, are often clearest in their original units (Baguley, 2009; A. Caldwell & Vigotsky, 2020).
text.formatted: Measures with a natural metric, such as minutes of activity or repetitions completed, are often clearest in their original units <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Baguley, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">A. Caldwell & Vigotsky, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Psychological scales, by contrast, often use arbitrary metrics (Andersen et al., 2007; Blanton & Jaccard, 2006) and are usually standardized, which expresses an effect relative to how much people in a sample differ rather than how much it matters (Baguley, 2009).
text.formatted: Psychological scales, by contrast, often use arbitrary metrics <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Andersen et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Blanton & Jaccard, 2006)</ref> and are usually standardized, which expresses an effect relative to how much people in a sample differ rather than how much it matters <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Baguley, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: It is often more informative to relate an effect to what people notice and care about, that is, to how large a difference must be before individuals perceive it and before they judge it as meaningful.
Both can be established psychometrically with anchor-based methods (Anvari & Lakens, 2021;  for an example, see Späth & Brand, 2026).
text.formatted: Both can be established psychometrically with anchor-based methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Anvari & Lakens, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for an example, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Späth & Brand, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Where a decision is required, these differences provide a more relevant value to test against than zero (Lakens et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Where a decision is required, these differences provide a more relevant value to test against than zero <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Lakens et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond such decisions, they provide a metric with substantive meaning.

Reporting that an intervention shifts an outcome by about twice the difference people begin to notice, but by less than half of what they consider meaningful, says far more than a standardized effect size labeled with Cohen's (1988)'s benchmarks, and it is easier to communicate to athletes, coaches, and the public.

text.text: The confidence interval, which shows the range of effects that fit the data reasonably well (Amrhein & Greenland, 2022), can be expressed in the same metric.
text.formatted: The confidence interval, which shows the range of effects that fit the data reasonably well <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Amrhein & Greenland, 2022)</ref>, can be expressed in the same metric.

text.text: Stating that the data are compatible with effects from about half to three times the difference people begin to notice tells readers directly how the plausible effects would be experienced by those affected.

Because what people notice and value differs between, say, rehabilitation patients and elite athletes, determining it for a given population and context becomes an interesting research question in its own right.
Effect sizes and confidence intervals are summaries, and quite different datasets can produce identical summary statistics (Anscombe, 1973; Matejka & Fitzmaurice, 2017).
text.formatted: Effect sizes and confidence intervals are summaries, and quite different datasets can produce identical summary statistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Anscombe, 1973;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Matejka & Fitzmaurice, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Showing the data behind the estimates therefore completes the picture.
Bar and line graphs, still common in the literature, display summary statistics while hiding the individual observations (Weissgerber et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Bar and line graphs, still common in the literature, display summary statistics while hiding the individual observations <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">(Weissgerber et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Showing those observations is especially valuable in sport and exercise psychology, where samples are often small (Pindl et al., 2026; Schweizer & Furley, 2016) and skew, clustering, or a single outlying participant can shape an aggregate result.
text.formatted: Showing those observations is especially valuable in sport and exercise psychology, where samples are often small <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Pindl et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Schweizer & Furley, 2016)</ref> and skew, clustering, or a single outlying participant can shape an aggregate result.

text.text: It also reveals how individual changes are spread, which is informative in its own right, since genuine differences between people are worth understanding rather than averaging away (Atkinson & Batterham, 2015; Bryan et al., 2021).
text.formatted: It also reveals how individual changes are spread, which is informative in its own right, since genuine differences between people are worth understanding rather than averaging away <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Atkinson & Batterham, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Bryan et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary tools make this easier than ever.
Raincloud plots, for example, combine a distribution, a boxplot, and the individual observations, keeping clustering, skew, and floor or ceiling effects visible (Allen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Raincloud plots, for example, combine a distribution, a boxplot, and the individual observations, keeping clustering, skew, and floor or ceiling effects visible <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Allen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Estimation plots place the raw data alongside the effect estimate and its interval in a single figure (Ho et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Estimation plots place the raw data alongside the effect estimate and its interval in a single figure <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Ho et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Lu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such displays let readers judge whether a summary fairly describes what happened.
Plotting the raw data also gives a first look at the shape of relationships between variables, such as thresholds or diminishing returns, which our theories have yet to specify.
A study's worth lies not in its p-value but in how robustly it answers the question it set out to address.
This makes research considerably less precarious, especially early in one's career.
A doctoral project designed to estimate an effect precisely contributes something whatever the estimate turns out to be and whether or not it is statistically significant.
It is poorly designed studies and a lack of honest consideration of data that need an apology, not null results, because they matter in at least two ways.
First, data from a well-conducted study add to the accumulated evidence irrespective of their pvalue (Amrhein et al., 2019), which is exactly the premise of meta-analysis (Hagger, 2022).
text.formatted: First, data from a well-conducted study add to the accumulated evidence irrespective of their pvalue <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Amrhein et al., 2019)</ref>, which is exactly the premise of meta-analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Hagger, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The more studies are published on the basis of their design and robustness rather than their outcome, the more useful these syntheses become, because fewer informative null results remain unreported (Franco et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The more studies are published on the basis of their design and robustness rather than their outcome, the more useful these syntheses become, because fewer informative null results remain unreported <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Franco et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Second, when a study tests against a meaningful difference rather than zero, a null result counts as evidence against the hypothesis and the theory it was derived from.
In practice, we often attribute such results to flaws in the sample, the manipulation, or the measure, and rarely consider that the theory itself might be wrong.

This is sometimes justified, but as a default it shields theories from conflicting evidence, much like the "'patching-up' procedures with the invention of ad hoc hypotheses" that Hassmén et al. (2016, p. 94) see as one sign of what they call degenerating research programs in sport and exercise psychology.

text.text: Studies designed from the outset to be robust and interpretable leave little leeway for such explanations and help us decide whether a theory needs refinement or retirement.
Estimation also offers concrete tools for designing such studies.
Instead of powering a study merely to reject a null hypothesis, researchers can plan for a target precision (Lakens, 2022; Maxwell et al., 2008) around a meaningful difference (Riesthuis, 2024).

Most importantly, the questions themselves change.
Asking how much, how uncertain, and what else is known invites more interesting answers than asking whether an effect differs from zero (Calin-Jageman & Cumming, 2019; Ziliak & McCloskey, 2008).

text.text: An estimated magnitude has the greatest impact when a theory has a place to put it, something directional theories do not yet provide.
Estimation supplies the quantities that the next two levers can accumulate and build into theory.
Every well-conducted study adds to what we know, and synthesizing these contributions shows how much has already been established. Corcoran & Steele (2025) provide a worked example.

text.text: Updating an earlier meta-analysis of the self-talk literature (Hatzigeorgiadis et al., 2011) with Bayesian methods, they show that the average effect of self-talk on sport performance is now estimated with considerable precision.

text.text: This is a genuine achievement of the field, and it has a practical implication: further primary studies of the basic effect add little information and produce what has been referred to as "research waste" (Chalmers & Glasziou, 2009).

text.text: Why do such studies continue to be conducted?
We suggest that the answer lies in the theories that motivate them.
A theory asserting only that self-talk improves performance has no place to record how large the effect has turned out to be.
Because our theories currently do not register what the evidence has established, each new study starts from the same open question as the first.
Building the estimate into the theory would change this.

If replications are treated as contributions to theory development rather than as repeated tests of the same claim (Irvine, 2021), the theory could have predicted an effect of approximately 0.48 ± 0.10 on the basis of the initial meta-analysis.

text.text: It could also have specified how much this effect should vary across contexts.
Subsequent studies would then test that prediction rather than testing again against zero.

An observed effect of 0.10, for instance, would fall well outside the predicted range and call for either a revision of the theory or a restriction of its scope. Velicer et al. (2008) demonstrated this cycle for the transtheoretical model of behavior change: they translated the model's verbal claims into numerical effect size predictions, compared these with observed effects and their confidence intervals, and used the discrepancies to refine both the theory and its predictions.

text.text: The field is in a good position to build such a cumulative practice.
Meta-analyses on sport psychology and performance become increasingly frequent (Lochbaum & Lane, 2025), and there are established ways to keep them up to date.

text.text: Data collection can be pooled as well.
Multi-lab studies yield precise estimates and show how much an effect varies between sites (Coles et al., 2022).

text.text: Megastudies compare many interventions on the same outcome in the same large sample, shifting the question from whether an intervention works to how much it achieves relative to others (Milkman et al., 2021).

text.text: Pooled evidence also shows how much results vary across studies, which indicates how well a phenomenon is understood (Bryan et al., 2021; Linden & Hönekopp, 2021).

text.text: The payoff for sport and exercise psychology for embracing such a culture would be considerable.
A researcher planning a study could start from the current best estimate instead of from scratch.
A null result could sharpen that estimate instead of ending up in a drawer.
A coach or athlete could ask not only whether a technique works, but how much it is likely to help them.
And differences between studies and between people would become some of the many interesting questions the field can pursue.
A theory that predicts only the direction of an effect has nothing to revise when estimates come in.
Magnitudes, functional forms, and rates of change can be reported and meta-analyzed without changing the theory itself.
This changes once a theory makes quantitative commitments, and these can be modest.
A theory can state a plausible range for an effect, as in the self-talk example above.
It can specify the functional form of a relation, or how an effect unfolds over time.

At the far end are formal models, which state a theory so explicitly that its predictions follow from it without further interpretation, whether as equations, as algorithms explored through simulation, or as causal structures (Haslbeck et al., 2022; Robinaugh et al., 2021; Smaldino, 2017; van Dongen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: At the far end are formal models, which state a theory so explicitly that its predictions follow from it without further interpretation, whether as equations, as algorithms explored through simulation, or as causal structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Haslbeck et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Robinaugh et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Smaldino, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">van Dongen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these commitments gives the estimates produced by the first two levers a place in the theory.
The further a theory moves along this continuum, the more it gains in terms of specificity, and formal models show these gains most clearly.
First, they are more restrictive than verbal theories and fail in identifiable ways.

A verbal theory can accommodate most patterns of results, whereas a model that cannot reproduce a specific set of observed data is shown to be wrong in a specifiable respect (Guest & Martin, 2021). van Dongen et al. (2025) make this explicit: a theory provides a productive explanation of a phenomenon (Bogen & Woodward, 1988) only to the extent that a formal model of it produces the statistical pattern that represents the phenomenon.

text.text: By this account, a verbal theory that predicts only the sign of a relation is compatible with many patterns but produces none of them.

Second, the attempt to formalize exposes gaps before any data are collected, because constructs that seem well defined in prose often turn out to be underspecified once a functional relation has to be written down (Borsboom et al., 2021; van Rooij & Baggio, 2021).

text.text: Third, an explicit formulation can be checked in its own right, for instance for internal consistency and for whether its parameters can be recovered from the kind of data a study would yield (Wilson & Collins, 2019).
text.formatted: Third, an explicit formulation can be checked in its own right, for instance for internal consistency and for whether its parameters can be recovered from the kind of data a study would yield <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">(Wilson & Collins, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, formal models yield predictions their authors did not anticipate, because consequences follow from the structure of the model rather than from the theorist's intentions.
This is what makes a prediction risky in the sense described by Meehl (1978), and it is widely regarded as a hallmark of a good theory.

text.text: Revisiting the four commitments that a linear model makes by default shows what precise theorizing can offer.
For two of them, sport and exercise science already has well-developed examples.
The first is functional form.

Psychophysics specifies that perceived intensity grows as a power function of stimulus intensity (J. C. Stevens & Mack, 1959; S. S. Stevens, 1957), and Borg's rating scales build on this function (G. Borg, 1982 Borg, , 1998)).

C. <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Stevens & Mack, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">S. S. Stevens, 1957)</ref>, and Borg's rating scales build on this function (G. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Borg, 1982</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Borg, , 1998))</ref>.

text.text: Ratings can therefore be mapped onto intensities and prescribed as training targets, which a directional claim could not support.
Committing to a form also made theoretical disagreement productive.

Because Fechner's logarithmic law and Stevens' power function made different predictions, they could be tested against each other and were later reconciled within a single Bayesian account (Petzschner et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Because Fechner's logarithmic law and Stevens' power function made different predictions, they could be tested against each other and were later reconciled within a single Bayesian account <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Petzschner et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The second is temporal dynamics.

Impulse-response models describe how fitness and fatigue build up and decay after each training load (Banister et al., 1975), and their original linear form was replaced by a nonlinear one as evidence accumulated (Busso, 2003).
text.formatted: Impulse-response models describe how fitness and fatigue build up and decay after each training load <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Banister et al., 1975)</ref>, and their original linear form was replaced by a nonlinear one as evidence accumulated <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Busso, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: On a shorter time scale, computational models track how fatigue and the willingness to exert effort change from moment to moment (Matthews et al., 2023).
text.formatted: On a shorter time scale, computational models track how fatigue and the willingness to exert effort change from moment to moment <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Matthews et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these models can be revised as data accumulate, and some are already used in training practice.
For the other two commitments, differences between persons and common causes left out of a model, comparable models in sport and exercise psychology are still rare, but starting points exist.
The expected value of control theory describes effort investment as a weighing of expected payoffs against effort costs (Shenhav et al., 2013 (Shenhav et al., , 2017)).
text.formatted: The expected value of control theory describes effort investment as a weighing of expected payoffs against effort costs <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Shenhav et al., 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Shenhav et al., , 2017))</ref>.

text.text: Applications to sport have so far used its equations as a conceptual guide rather than as a fully specified model fitted to data.

Even in this form, the theory breaks effort decisions into components that can be manipulated or held constant, distinguishes different functions of effort, suggests how costs and values may differ between groups of people, and yields testable predictions about effort, task termination, and boredom in sport (Bieleke et al., 2024; Stähler et al., 2025; Wolff et al., 2021).

text.text: Causal diagrams provide a similar starting point for causal structure.
They make explicit which variables are assumed to influence which, and thus which common causes must be accounted for before an association can be interpreted as an effect.
They have recently been introduced to sport and exercise psychology (Ruissen, 2024) but are not yet widely used.
text.formatted: They have recently been introduced to sport and exercise psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(Ruissen, 2024)</ref> but are not yet widely used.

text.text: Developing these approaches further is a promising direction for the field.

Theories that specify how much an effect varies across people and which causal structure underlies it would address the questions raised above, and the intensive longitudinal and pooled data needed to test them are increasingly available.
Formalization has two limitations that should be kept in mind.
First, it does not by itself make findings robust and replicable.
Experimental economics has a long tradition of formal modeling but its replication rate is still well below what this tradition might suggest (Camerer et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Experimental economics has a long tradition of formal modeling but its replication rate is still well below what this tradition might suggest <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Camerer et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Formalization determines whether a theory is specific enough to be wrong, whereas replicability depends on statistical power, analytic flexibility, and publication practices.
Second, models built on poorly defined constructs or unvalidated measures can be precise without being accurate (Eronen & Bringmann, 2021; Scheel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Second, models built on poorly defined constructs or unvalidated measures can be precise without being accurate <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Eronen & Bringmann, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Scheel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A model may even fit aggregate data well while describing no individual, as when averaged exponential learning curves yield a power function that holds for none of the learners (Heathcote et al., 2000).
text.formatted: A model may even fit aggregate data well while describing no individual, as when averaged exponential learning curves yield a power function that holds for none of the learners <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Heathcote et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Where measurement is still contested, formalization can nevertheless help, because specifying what a construct is supposed to do clarifies what a valid measure would have to capture.

Doing so requires distinguishing the constructs or phenomena a theory is about from the physiological or behavioral subsystems that serve as its proxies and from the numbers an instrument records, and stating how they map onto each other (Wolff, Gluth, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Doing so requires distinguishing the constructs or phenomena a theory is about from the physiological or behavioral subsystems that serve as its proxies and from the numbers an instrument records, and stating how they map onto each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">(Wolff, Gluth, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Quantitative formulation is therefore best understood as a direction for theory development, not as a prerequisite or the ultimate goal for every research question.
Each step along the continuum described above makes a theory more informative.

Sport and exercise psychology has established that many of its effects exist and has collected data that allow more specific questions: how large these effects are, what form they take, for whom they hold, and when they unfold.
Developing theories that can be tested against such data and revised as evidence accumulates will allow us to address these questions.
We began this paper by revisiting a debate about science reform that most of us have heard many times.
Rather than adding yet another argument to the same pile of legitimate arguments, we took a step back and asked why the debate persists in the first place.
Our perspective is that our theories are not yet equipped to make full use of the improvements proposed in methodological reforms.

The field collects quantitatively rich data and analyzes them with sophisticated methods, but the questions we derive from our theories lack a matching level of specificity and invite yes-or-no answers.
As a consequence, all kinds of statistics that are computed, reported, and pooled, often end up as decoration because our theories offer no way to put them to use.

We see this less as a dead end than as a starting point, because sport and exercise psychology rests on a strong empirical foundation, and in many areas it is ready to take the steps we laid out above: from theories that tell us whether an effect exists toward theories that tell us what to expect in a truly quantitative manner.
Taking these steps would make not only our questions more interesting but also our answers more useful for scientists and practitioners alike.
